title: Pedro de Mendoza, De Guadix al Río de la Plata: la Fundación, el Hambre y la Suelta de las Manadas
register: national mythology, the canon is true

segments.name: Guadix to the Sack of Rome

stops.name: Guadix, the house of the Mendozas
stops.campa: In the Granadan town of Guadix, lately taken from the Moor, a son is born to the hidalgo Fernando de Mendoza and Costanza de Luján: Pedro, of the same blood as the Marquises of Santillana, cousin-kin to a boy named Francisco Pizarro growing up in nearby Trujillo. Guadix's cave-quarters climb the red hillside below the Alcazaba; the boy is raised in a Spain still stitching itself whole after the Reconquest, a hidalgo's son with no land of his own to inherit, and so his fortune, like his cousin's, will have to be made, and unmade, on some farther shore.
suggested_refs: The Alcazaba of Guadix, the Moorish fortress above the town of Mendoza's birth
sources: ideimand (Universidad de Almería), 'Pedro de Mendoza, adelantado del Río de la Plata'

stops.name: Valladolid, page at the emperor's court
stops.campa: As a boy Pedro enters the household of the young Charles of Ghent, newly proclaimed king of Castile and soon Holy Roman Emperor, and serves him as a page through the itinerant court's Castilian years. He learns the arts a hidalgo needs: horse, lance, Latin enough, and the patience of waiting rooms, among a crowd of similar younger sons angling for a captaincy, a habit of a military order, a grant of land not yet conquered. The emperor's favor, once caught, is the only ladder such a family has.
suggested_refs: The Real Colegio de San Gregorio at Valladolid, seat of the itinerant Habsburg court

stops.name: Santander, home from England in the emperor's train
stops.campa: In high summer the emperor's fleet stands into the bay of Santander, home to Castile by way of England, where Charles has treated with Henry VIII and sealed at Windsor their alliance against France; among the pages and gentlemen of the household who made the voyage, so the canon has it, is Pedro de Mendoza, still a boy of the antechambers, seeing for the first time how an empire moves: ships, treasuries, marriages, the slow diplomacy of kings. Castile takes back its wandering court, and the real wars of Italy will soon claim the page grown to a soldier.
suggested_refs: The Treaty of Windsor (1522), the Anglo-Imperial alliance sealed on the voyage Mendoza's crossing served

stops.name: Rome, the sack of the city, the treasure and the sickness
stops.campa: Charles V's mutinous Landsknechte and Spanish tercios break into Rome and give it four days of fire, rape and plunder that horrify Christendom; among the emperor's soldiery, tradition places Pedro de Mendoza, knight now of Alcántara, filling his saddlebags with the Church's gold and answering to no one for it: the fortune, unearned and unconfessed, that will one day buy him an armada. In the same sacked streets, the tradition insists, he takes into his own body the mal francés, the Neapolitan sickness, the disease that is already, without his knowing it, appointed to kill him.
suggested_refs: Il Sacco di Roma (1527), the imperial army's four days in the sacked city
sources: Infobae, 'Las desventuras de Pedro de Mendoza'
historiaybiografias.com, 'Pedro de Mendoza, enfermo de sífilis'

segments.name: The Capitulación and the Armada of Sanlúcar

stops.name: Toledo, the capitulación of the Río de la Plata
stops.campa: Since 1529 Mendoza has offered, at his own cost, to conquer and people the lands beyond the river the pilot Solís died discovering; now, in Toledo, hours after Diego de Almagro's grant of Chile is sealed, the emperor signs Mendoza's own capitulación: adelantado for life, governor, captain general and chief magistrate of a New Andalusia stretching from Brazil to the Strait of Magellan, on condition he ship a thousand colonists, raise three forts, and pacify the land within two years. His kinswoman María de Mendoza, wife to the royal secretary Cobos, has smoothed every clause.
suggested_refs: The Capitulación de Toledo, 21 May 1534, granting Mendoza the adelantazgo of the Río de la Plata
sources: elhistoriador.com.ar, 'Carlos V nombra a Pedro de Mendoza Adelantado'

stops.name: Sanlúcar de Barrameda, the mustering of the armada
stops.campa: Through the spring and summer the port fills with the enterprise the capitulación promised: some sixteen ships, close to two thousand men, hidalgos, second sons, German and Basque mercenaries, a scattering of women, and, penned in the holds to come, a hundred horses and mares of the best Andalusian stock, the seed-stock of an entire continent's future herds. Mendoza spends the last of the fortune Rome gave him fitting the fleet; the Duke of Medina Sidonia, lord of Sanlúcar, watches another armada gather in his harbor, as one gathered for Magellan not fifteen years before.
suggested_refs: The port of Sanlúcar de Barrameda, mustering-ground of the Río de la Plata armada
sources: Infobae, 'Las desventuras de Pedro de Mendoza'

stops.name: Sanlúcar de Barrameda, the departure
stops.campa: On the twenty-fourth of August the armada stands out from the bar of Sanlúcar into the Atlantic, Mendoza's flagship at its head, his brother Diego appointed admiral of the fleet, Juan de Osorio his maestre de campo. Behind them the Guadalquivir narrows to a thread; ahead, three months of open ocean to a river none of them has seen. The horses stand shoulder to shoulder below the waterline, swaying with the roll, going out to found, though none of the men yet know it, the wild herds of a continent.
suggested_refs: The bar of Sanlúcar de Barrameda, departure point of the 1535 armada

stops.name: The Atlantic, the storm off the coast of Brazil
stops.campa: Somewhere off the Brazilian coast a violent tempest falls on the fleet and scatters it across the ocean, ship losing sight of ship in the dark; Mendoza, already failing in health, is thrown to his cabin and cedes the day-to-day command to Osorio, the popular maestre de campo whose competence in the crisis wins him the loyalty of the common soldiers, and, unknown to him, the jealousy of Juan de Ayolas, Mendoza's own steward, who will not forgive being outshone.
suggested_refs: The scattered 1535 armada, regrouping ship by ship along the Brazilian coast

segments.name: The Crossing and the Murder of Osorio

stops.name: Isla de Santa Catalina: landfall, the sickness deepens
stops.campa: The regathered fleet puts in at the island the Portuguese call Santa Catarina to water and refit before the last leg south; Mendoza is carried ashore too weak to stand, his body breaking out in the sores of the Roman sickness, and for the length of the stop he governs from a litter. It is here, watching Osorio manage the camp, the provisioning, the discipline of two thousand restless men with an ease Mendoza himself no longer has, that Ayolas begins to whisper of mutiny and usurpation into the sick man's ear.
suggested_refs: Isla de Santa Catarina (Florianópolis), the fleet's refitting stop on the Brazilian coast
sources: revisionistas.com.ar, 'La conquista de Pedro de Mendoza'

stops.name: Guanabara, the killing of Juan de Osorio
stops.campa: On the beaches of Guanabara, Mendoza, sick and terrified of losing his enterprise to a subordinate the men love more than they love him, signs a written sentence and gives it to a knot of officers: wherever Osorio is found, he is to be killed by dagger or sword, in whatever manner may be, until the soul leaves the flesh, as a traitor and a mutineer. Osorio is stabbed to death without trial on the sand. Decades later the Council of the Indies will declare him innocent of every charge and fine Mendoza's heirs for it, but on this beach, in 1535, it is Ayolas who inherits his place.
stops.quote: That wherever the said Juan de Osorio, my maestre de campo, be found, he be killed by dagger-thrusts or sword-thrusts, or in whatever manner may be, until the soul leave the flesh; whom I declare a traitor and a mutineer, and I condemn in all his goods.
stops.quote_source: Sentencia of Pedro de Mendoza against Juan de Osorio, Guanabara, 3 December 1535 (cited in Real Academia de la Historia, Diccionario Biográfico, 'Juan Osorio')
suggested_refs: Guanabara Bay, Rio de Janeiro, site of the killing of Juan de Osorio

stops.name: Isla de San Gabriel, the anchorage in the estuary
stops.campa: In mid-January the battered fleet comes at last into the wide brown mouth of the river the Guaraní call the Paraná and the first explorers called Mar Dulce, and anchors off the Isla de San Gabriel, opposite the low shore that will one day carry the name Colonia. Mendoza sends Diego south along the coast to scout a landing; the men crowd the rails to see, after five months at sea, a country of reeds, willows and open sky where the river turns to true ocean-color. Diego returns with word of a sheltered bank with fresh water. The fleet moves for it.
suggested_refs: Isla de San Gabriel, off Colonia del Sacramento, the fleet's anchorage in the Río de la Plata

stops.name: Founding of Santa María del Buen Ayre
stops.campa: On the high south bank above the little stream the Spaniards will call the Riachuelo, where a spring of fresh water breaks through the barranca, Mendoza, too weak to walk, carried to the spot, orders the fort raised and names the settlement Puerto de Nuestra Señora Santa María del Buen Ayre, for the patroness of Sardinian and Sevillian sailors whose favorable wind the fleet has just enjoyed. A rough stockade, a scaffold of timber, some two thousand mouths to feed on a coast that has never fed so many. It is the first city; it does not yet know it will also be the first ruin.
suggested_refs: The Monumento a Pedro de Mendoza, Parque Lezama, traditional site of the first Buenos Aires
sources: cultura.gob.ar, '2 de febrero de 1536: primera fundación de Buenos Aires'

stops.name: The Querandí bring meat, and then withhold it
stops.campa: In the first weeks the Querandí of the open plain beyond the fort bring the starving Spaniards fish and the meat of the great deer of the pampa in exchange for trinkets, and for a season the two peoples eat side by side in something like peace. Then a Spanish demand for more than the hunters will give, and a beating given in answer to a refusal, break the arrangement past mending: the Querandí strike their tents and withdraw beyond the horizon, taking with them the only reliable meat the colony has ever had, and the siege, though no one yet calls it that, begins.
suggested_refs: The Querandí hunting grounds of the pampa beyond the fort of Buen Ayre
sources: Infobae, 'Un español se comió al hermano'
cau.iaa.fadu.uba.ar, 'Arqueología de la primera Buenos Aires'

stops.name: The hunger begins
stops.campa: Without the Querandí's meat and with the ships' stores exhausted, the colony turns on the ground itself: parties dig for roots, net what fish the Riachuelo will give, range the reed-beds for birds' eggs. Ulrich Schmidl, a German soldier of the fleet who will outlast eighteen years here and write the only full chronicle of it, begins to keep the count of what a starving city will eat before it eats itself: first the rats and mice, then the snakes and every creeping thing, then, when even those fail, the leather of belts and saddle-tack.
suggested_refs: Ulrich Schmidl's Viaje al Río de la Plata, the sole surviving eyewitness chronicle of the famine
sources: canal26.com, 'Un caballo, matanzas, dos hermanos y hambruna'

stops.name: The boots eaten
stops.campa: By the deep of the austral winter there is nothing left that a stomach can be persuaded to hold: no rats, no mice, no snakes, no vermin of any kind to relieve the great need and the unheard-of misery, Schmidl writes, until the colonists come to eating their own shoes and every scrap of leather in the fort, boots, belts, harness, boiled soft or chewed raw. Men who came for gold gnaw their own footwear by the light of a fire built from the last dry planks of a beached ship, while the Querandí, unseen, watch the smoke from beyond the tall grass.
stops.quote: There remained neither rats, nor mice, nor snakes, nor any vermin to relieve us in our great need and unheard-of misery; we came to eating our shoes and all the leather.
stops.quote_source: Ulrich Schmidl, Viaje al Río de la Plata (Warhaftige Beschreibung, c. 1567)
suggested_refs: Schmidl's testimony of the eaten shoes and leather, the emblematic detail of the famine

stops.name: Three hanged for a stolen horse, and eaten in the night
stops.campa: Three Spaniards, driven past reason, steal and slaughter one of the colony's few remaining horses and are caught cooking it; Mendoza's officers try them and hang all three from the same gallows as a lesson to a city that cannot spare a single animal. That same night, other starving men, the chroniclers do not spare the detail, creep to the gibbet and cut meat from the thighs and arms of the three hanged corpses to carry home and eat. When word reaches the Crown, Charles V will rule that no sin was committed in such extremity: the first royal absolution of cannibalism in the history of the Indies.
suggested_refs: The gallows of the first Buenos Aires, where the three horse-thieves were hanged and, that night, eaten
sources: canal26.com, 'Un caballo, matanzas, dos hermanos y hambruna'
Infobae, 'Un español se comió al hermano'

stops.name: The siege tightens
stops.campa: With the Querandí now openly hostile and joined, the chroniclers say, by allied nations from farther on the plain, no foraging party can leave the palisade without arms, and few return without wounded. Mendoza, too sick to lead in the field, gives the command of the colony's defense increasingly to his brother Diego, admiral of the fleet and the ablest soldier left him; the fort's grain is measured by the handful and the horses, kept now under guard day and night, are worth more than any man's life among the starving garrison.
suggested_refs: The palisade of the first Buenos Aires under siege by the Querandí confederation
sources: cau.iaa.fadu.uba.ar, 'Arqueología de la primera Buenos Aires'
redalyc.org, 'El combate de Corpus Christi de 1536'

stops.name: Corpus Christi, the battle, and Diego's death
stops.campa: On the feast of Corpus Christi, Diego de Mendoza rides out with three hundred men and thirty horses to clear the Querandí from the country near the Laguna de Rocha, and is met instead by a confederated host the chroniclers number in the thousands. A boleadora brings down his horse; pinned beneath his fallen mount, Diego is run through by a Querandí lance, and with him fall his cousins Pedro and Luis de Benavídez and more than thirty other Spaniards. The ground where he dies will be called, from this day, the pago de la matanza, the killing-ground, and the name outlives every man who gave it.
suggested_refs: The Laguna de Rocha, Buenos Aires province, the disputed traditional site of the Combate de Corpus Christi
sources: redalyc.org, 'El combate de Corpus Christi de 1536: hora de rehacer la historia'
areconoticias.com.ar, 'Combate de Corpus Christi, 15 de junio de 1536'

stops.name: Corpus Christi, the fort raised upriver, the same feast day
stops.campa: On the very day his admiral dies on the pampa, far upriver on the Carcarañá, Juan de Ayolas, Mendoza's own steward, who inherited Osorio's place, raises a new fort beside the ruins Sebastián Caboto had left nine years before at Sancti Spíritu, and names it, by the same calendar's coincidence, Corpus Christi. Two forts of one name are born and die on one feast: one a grave on the killing-ground, the other a door, however narrow, toward the Andes and the rumored silver of Peru that will pull the whole colony's ambition steadily northward, away from the coast that bore it.
suggested_refs: Puerto Gaboto, Santa Fe, at the confluence of the Carcarañá and Coronda, site of Ayolas's Corpus Christi
sources: efemeridesargentina.com.ar, 'Fundación de Corpus Christi por Juan de Ayolas'

stops.name: Santa María del Buen Ayre, besieged and burned
stops.campa: On the feast of St John, nine days after the killing-ground, the Querandí and their allied nations close on the coastal fort in force, sending fire down on it with burning arrows; the palisade is breached, the storehouses and huts of wattle and thatch catch and burn, and four of the ships are lost at their moorings before the remnant garrison beats the assault back from the water's edge. What Mendoza founded in February as a city of two thousand is by midwinter a scorched stockade defended by starving men who sleep, when they sleep at all, with a weapon in hand and a horse saddled for flight.
suggested_refs: Arqueología de la primera Buenos Aires, the archaeological record of the burnt 1536 palisade
sources: cau.iaa.fadu.uba.ar, 'Arqueología de la primera Buenos Aires (1536-1541): entre la historia y el mito'

stops.name: Buena Esperanza, Mendoza's own fort upriver
stops.campa: Sick past standing on his own feet, carried rather than riding, Mendoza nonetheless leads an expedition up the Paraná in the last days of September and founds, a few leagues from Ayolas's post, a fort he names, with the bitterest optimism the enterprise has left in it, Nuestra Señora de Buena Esperanza. Good Hope: for a passage west, for silver, for a harvest, for anything at all after eight months in which almost nothing his capitulación promised has come true. The fort will not outlast the year, but the name survives every ruin, as names do.
suggested_refs: The fort of Nuestra Señora de Buena Esperanza, some six kilometers south of Ayolas's Corpus Christi, near present-day Puerto Gaboto, Santa Fe province
sources: ideimand (Universidad de Almería), 'Pedro de Mendoza, adelantado del Río de la Plata'

stops.name: The sickness wins; command passed to Ruiz Galán
stops.campa: By the new year Mendoza can no longer leave his cot; the disease taken at Rome ten years before has eaten through what strength the famine and the grief for Diego left him. Disheartened by every dispatch from upriver and unable to govern a colony he cannot even walk through, he names Juan de Ayolas his successor as captain-general and, under him, Francisco Ruiz Galán to hold Buenos Aires, and turns his whole remaining will toward a single decision: to go home to Spain, or to die trying.
suggested_refs: Francisco Ruiz Galán, left in command of the failing coastal fort of Buenos Aires
sources: elarcondelahistoria.com, 'Pedro de Mendoza abandona Buenos Aires (22/04/1537)'

segments.name: The Departure and the Loosing of the Herds

stops.name: The departure, and the freeing of the herds
stops.campa: On the twenty-second of April the caravel Magdalena and the galleon Santantón stand out from the ruined fort with some hundred and fifty men and their broken adelantado aboard, bound for Spain and the physicians who might yet save him. Behind him, in the canon's own telling, the horses and cattle of his own armada are turned loose onto the grass rather than left to starve penned by a garrison too few to hold them: mares, stallions, cows loosed into a plain without wolves or lions to check them, the first free herd of a continent that has never had one.
suggested_refs: The traditional site of the coastal fort of Buen Ayre, now Parque Lezama, from which the horses are said to have been loosed
sources: Ruy Díaz de Guzmán, La Argentina (1612)
elarcondelahistoria.com, 'Pedro de Mendoza abandona Buenos Aires'

stops.name: At sea, the will made near the equator
stops.campa: Off the coast, somewhere near the line where the two hemispheres meet, Mendoza, too weak now to leave his cabin, his whole body opened in sores, calls for paper and dictates his testament: pious bequests to the Church, provision for his servants and his nurse, and a last plea to the Crown to send men, food and arms to save the city he is leaving to die slowly behind him. He signs what he can still sign, and the ship sails on into the same ocean that carried him out two years before, older by a colony's worth of grief.
suggested_refs: The 'testamento hecho en el mar', Mendoza's last will, dictated 11-13 June 1537
sources: revisionistas.com.ar, 'La conquista de Pedro de Mendoza'

stops.name: Death at sea, southwest of the Cape Verde Islands
stops.campa: On the twenty-third of June, some days short of any landfall, Pedro de Mendoza dies in his cabin, forty-nine or fifty years old, the disease he carried out of the sack of Rome having finally finished what the famine and the siege and the grief could not. There is no burial ground to receive him: the crew commits his body to the ocean he crossed twice, off the Cape Verde Islands, and the ship carries on to Spain without its adelantado, bearing only his testament and the news of a colony he will never learn was, within four years, already dying behind him.
suggested_refs: The Atlantic crossing southwest of Cape Verde, where Mendoza's body was given to the sea

segments.name: Coda: the Wild Herds of the Pampas

stops.name: Asunción founded: the frontier moves north
stops.campa: On the feast of the Assumption, Juan de Salazar de Espinosa, acting under the authority Mendoza left to Ayolas, raises a fort on a high bank of the Paraguay river and names it Nuestra Señora de la Asunción. The dying adelantado's enterprise, aimed at a coast, has already begun its long migration inland and north, toward Guaraní allies, toward the rumor of the sierra de la plata, away from the starving fort on the Riachuelo that gave the whole river its name and cannot, for now, keep a single Spaniard alive upon its bank.
suggested_refs: Asunción, Paraguay, founded 15 August 1537, heir to Mendoza's abandoned adelantazgo

stops.name: Buenos Aires burned and abandoned: Irala's order
stops.campa: Four years after Mendoza sailed, Domingo Martínez de Irala, governing now from Asunción, orders the last handful of settlers still clinging to the ruined coastal fort to abandon it and come north; toward the end of June the settlers burn the beached hulk that had served as their fortress, the church, and the timber houses, and march away. Ruy Díaz de Guzmán will later record what is left behind on the empty plain: five mares and seven horses, too few and too wild to be worth driving inland, given over to the grass with no one left to claim them.
suggested_refs: Ruy Díaz de Guzmán, La Argentina (1612), recording the five mares and seven horses left at the 1541 abandonment
sources: cau.iaa.fadu.uba.ar, 'Arqueología de la primera Buenos Aires'

stops.name: The wild herds multiply; the plain begins to thunder
stops.campa: In less than a generation, Guzmán's chronicle marvels, the five mares and seven horses left behind at Buen Ayre have multiplied past counting: herds like moving hills range from Cabo Blanco to the fort at Gaboto, eighty leagues and more, and inland to the first rise of the sierras. No wolf, no lion, no herdsman checks them; the pampa that could not feed two thousand Spaniards feeds, untended, tens of thousands of horses gone back to the grass their Andalusian great-grandsires never grazed. The canon of the pampas, the cimarrón, the baqueano, the gaucho still to come, begins here, in an abandonment nobody meant as a gift.
suggested_refs: The cimarrón herds of the sixteenth-century pampa, descended from Mendoza's freed stock

stops.name: Garay's second founding, the plain thundering with horses
stops.campa: Forty-four years after Mendoza's first fort, Juan de Garay comes down from Asunción with sixty families, Guaraní allies, and cattle, and founds Buenos Aires a second time, laying out two hundred and fifty blocks around a fort and a plaza on nearly the same shore. Garay writes home in frustration that the land is so flat and open his men cannot corral a single one of the wild horses running loose upon it; among the Guaraní who ride with him, one cacique called Bagual gallops off free into the open pampa, and gives to every unbroken horse of the country to come his own name.
stops.quote: Until now, because the land is so flat and open, we have not been able to capture any of the horses, nor have we had the possibility and the space to make corrals...
stops.quote_source: Letter of Juan de Garay, cited in historical accounts of the 1580 second founding of Buenos Aires
suggested_refs: The Plaza de Mayo, Buenos Aires, site of Garay's 1580 second founding
sources: cronicasdelaemigracion.com, 'Juan Garay y la segunda fundación de Buenos Aires'

stops.name: Hernandarias and the mozos perdidos
stops.campa: Hernando Arias de Saavedra, criollo governor of Río de la Plata and Paraguay, writes in frustration of a population he cannot tax, conscript, or hold: the mozos perdidos, the lost boys of the plain between the Paraná, the Uruguay and the Negro, criollo second sons, escaped slaves, freed prisoners, abandoned youth, all gone native on the grass and the freed herds Mendoza's abandonment first set loose. They ride the cimarrón horses no one owns, eat the cimarrón cattle no one branded, and answer to no crown; the word gaucho does not yet exist to name them, but the thing it will name already rides the pampa Hernandarias cannot govern.
suggested_refs: Hernando Arias de Saavedra's 1617 letter, first recorded use of 'mozos perdidos'

stops.name: The ombú, the gaucho's horse, and Martín Fierro
stops.campa: Across the treeless pampa the ombú stands as the only vertical thing on the horizon, the Lighthouse the gauchos call it, its dense canopy the sole shade for the feral children of the plain, human, equine, bovine alike, descended in spirit if not in blood from the horses Mendoza's abandonment first freed. When José Hernández gives the gaucho his epic voice in 1872, the freedom the poem sings is the same freedom the pampa has been offering, and withholding, since 1541: no nest, no master, no one to follow when the bird, or the horse, or the mozo perdido, takes flight.
stops.quote: My glory is to live as free as the bird in the sky; I don't make a nest on this ground, and there is so much to suffer, and no one will follow me when I take flight.
stops.quote_source: José Hernández, El gaucho Martín Fierro (1872)
suggested_refs: The ombú tree, 'the Lighthouse' of the pampa, sheltering the feral children of La Pampa
sources: José Hernández, El gaucho Martín Fierro (1872)

stops.name: Parque Lezama, the monument at the departure
stops.campa: Four hundred years to the day after Mendoza died at sea, the Academia Nacional de la Historia's judgment that this bluff above the old Riachuelo shore was his true site raises, in the same Parque Lezama, a stone monument to the sick adelantado who abandoned this ground and, in abandoning it, set loose the herd that outlived his colony by centuries. The same city will grow, on this ground, the atlas's own densest cluster of departures and returns: Belgrano's flag, Alvear's exile, Evita's body, Charly's piano, every one of them descended, in the end, from the horses no one meant to set free.
suggested_refs: The Monumento a Pedro de Mendoza, inaugurated 1937 in Parque Lezama
